utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. Defence teams I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic, Mrs. Nikolic, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Krgovic. No, Mr. Haynes is here. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye present. I understand there are no preliminaries so good afternoon, everyone. Witness is present. Good afternoon, to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be saying the truth, speaking the truth. Madam usher is going to hand you the text of the declaration, solemn declaration, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Bourgon will introduce himself better to you, will be putting some questions to you. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Bourgon. One moment because there is a lot, a lot of background noise. Okay. It seems to be gone now. No. I can still hear it. This has a lot of interference. How is your -- let's try this one. If the interference is such that you cannot continue Mr. Bourgon, please draw our attention immediately. Thank you. As far as it goes now it seems to be okay. But you never know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President, good afternoon judges, good afternoon colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the record allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon and along with me colleague today, Ms. Marie-Claude Fournie, we represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. Can I ask you first to begin by stating your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Milisav Cvijetinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, before we begin, I would like simply to remind you that I will be asking a number of questions and if at any time you do not understand the question, don't hesitate to ask me to either say the question again or to clarify my question. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what is your date of birth and your age?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: 10th of April 1963. I'm 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Vitinica, the Bourgeon [phoen] hamlet in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before the war, sir, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I am construction worker.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me what I did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war I worked in Belgrade in a construction company Dom and I also worked abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where abroad did you work before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Israel, in Russia, and in Brazil.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you have any prior military service before the war in your country?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where was that and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I served in Zagreb and I was -- I was in communications, in signals, that was my military occupational specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that was with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the war where were you? Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: During the war -- I was in Israel when the war broke out, and then after I received news that my family had moved out and that my village was burned down, I went back to rejoin my family and I remained with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where exactly did you remain with your family after you returned?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I was in a Muslim house in the village of Skocici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have any children at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had two children. Three years old, that was my elder child and my younger child was two months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, today, sir, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I do the same job I had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand that during the war you were mobilised within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I understand also that you were a member of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you serve with any battalion in particular within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you do within the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I was a communications man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus on the year of 1995, more particularly July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you recall this period, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where was the command of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: In Malesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as a communicator where did you work?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The same place, Malesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did the battalion have a communication centre?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was it in the same building as the command or a separate building?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were some 50 metres away from the battalion command in a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is where you worked yourself as a communicator?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You recall if following the fall of Srebrenica you were on duty during this period?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the communications centre at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how did the duty shifts work during this period?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were five- or seven-day breaks except if there was a state of standby, then we were on standby. If news came that there would be an attack then we would all be there, the full complement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many communicators were working in that communication centre, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did all the communicators work at the same place in the same communication centre?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Two communicators were in the communication centre and one of them was at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's the forward command post of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where were your sleeping accommodations?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: We slept in the communications centre, those of us who were there manning the communications center, and that person who was at the forward command post slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You responded to my question that there were three communicators. Is that the total number of communicators in the battalion command or is that those who were on duty?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were more of us but those were just the persons who were there at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you were on duty following the fall of Srebrenica, that was in the communication centre located close to the command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned the battalion forward command post or IKM. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: It was at Pecine where our defences were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the commander of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sreco Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall how many companies were in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how did the command of the battalion communicate with the companies?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion command communicated with the companies through the communication centre, through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that by radio or by phone?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: By phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what kind of telephones were these?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Military induction phones. It was a wire type phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So just to be precise, was this or these phones wire or wireless?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who had a phone like this or where were these phones?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion command, the company commanders and the logistics had those phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was there a phone like that in the IKM?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If a company commander wanted to call the battalion command, can you explain what the procedure he would have to follow, how did this work?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: If a company commander wanted to call the battalion commander he first had to call us in the communication centre, I would respond, and then I contacted the -- I got into contact with the battalion commander or whoever it was that they wanted to talk to and then I simply put them in contact, and that's how they were able to speak to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And now, what if the battalion command or somebody in the battalion command wanted to speak to a company commander, what was the procedure then?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The same principle. The battalion command calls the switchboard, and then tell us what company they wanted to get in touch with, I call the company and I put the battalion command through to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when I look at this communications system between the battalion command and the companies, were such communicators reliable at the time? Or maybe if I can be more precise, did you have any problems with this communication system at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there would be a disruption if there was shelling, then the lines could be disrupted. But then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer. He is also kindly asked to speak more slowly and clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, shall I leave this in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The interpreter ask you to speak a bit more slower and to try and speak more clearly between the words so that they can better interpret. You mentioned some disruptions on the line due to shelling and then you added something that the interpreters did not get. So what would happen if there was, for example, like you say, disruption on those lines.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: If there was a disruption then one of the signalmen would remain in the centre and the other one would go out to the line and would link up with the man at the forward command post to the place where the disruption occurred and would fix it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you say, "the man at the forward command post," I take it you mean the communicator who was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the signal man or the communicator.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to turn to communications between the battalion command and the brigade command. How did that work?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the principle was the same. If the battalion command wanted to speak to the brigade command they had to call us at the centre and then I called the brigade centre in order to put the battalion command through to them so that they could talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And let's just to make it clear for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom, if the battalion commander wanted to speak to the duty officer in the brigade command, can you describe step by step how this would be done?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion command calls the communication centre. I in turn call the com centre at the brigade, and I put them in touch with the battalion command and then the battalion command talks to their signalman and asks them to call whoever it is that they want to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, there were four persons involved in such a communication?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The one who is making the call, I who put them through, and then the signal man in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if a call was coming from the brigade command to the battalion command using that phone system that you described for us, who is the first person to get this call at the battalion, to hear this call?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: It's the same principle. If somebody calls from the brigade command and they want to talk to somebody in the 2nd Battalion again it goes through the com centre, through us, and I call the 2nd Battalion and whoever is there at the 2nd Battalion picks up, the battalion commander, the personnel officer, whoever it there and then they pick up the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a civilian phone in the communication centre where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To your knowledge was there a civilian phone in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is it possible on the lines of communication that you describe for the enemy to intercept these communications?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why is that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Because all the lines were in our territory. There was no line crossing into their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what would someone have to do in order to intercept these communications?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they'd have to put some bugging equipment on the wire and then eavesdrop on the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, these wires that you discuss, and whether it is between the companies and the battalion command or between the battalion command and the brigade command, did they sometimes break?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move to a different area concerning the communications centre. Was there a radio in your communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of radio that was?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: It was RUP 12 radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was there a radio in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you familiar back in 1995 with the procedure for sending or receiving a telegram at the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the procedure when a telegram is received from the brigade? Maybe let's begin first by what is a telegram, can you describe for us what is meant by the word telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: A telegram is a written piece of text containing information who the sender is and who is on the receiving end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how is this written, you say, information communicated? Or transmitted, maybe to use a better word.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: When communicating in this way, when, for example, a brigade commander is sending a message to the 2nd Battalion, their signalsman calls the switchboard at the 2nd Battalion and then the message is dictated and taken down. Once that is completed, the person from the 2nd Battalion who responded is then being told the message word for word and taken down -- the message gets taken down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it is the communicator in the communications centre who notes down the telegram that is dictated to him, is that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how is this information -- can you describe to the best of your recollection how is this information then communicated to the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Perfectly. Once the communicator has heard the telegram and noted it down, as you describe, what does he do next?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He delivers it to the person who is supposed to receive it, for example, at the battalion command. If in turn the battalion command wants to send a message to the brigade commander, then the brigade commander would finally receive the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in between the communications centre and the battalion command, is that done orally using the phone, or is that delivery in paper?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Between the com centre and the battalion we used telephone lines. If at the battalion command, there's only one duty officer and cannot take the message down himself, then, for example, I would do it and hand it over personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you know, was the telegram transmitted by phone written down by somebody in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Everything I dictate over the phone, they take down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if a telegram is sent by the brigade command using the military phone, the first person to hear the content of the telegram within the battalion, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The first person to hear it, you mean in the battalion? The battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I will make my question more precise. Within the battalion lines, the first person to hear the message which is dictated, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: It would be us, the signalsmen. We were the ones receiving the telegram and forwarding it to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as a signalman or communicator, did you use codes to encrypt telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was there, to your knowledge, a book in the communications centre which explained to you how to code or decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, were you qualified, did you have the knowledge to code or decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you were a communicator in the JNA. Did you learn then how to code or decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the other communicators in the 2nd Battalion qualified or have the knowledge to code or decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's no basis, there's no foundation laid for the question. The answer at this stage would be purely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness knows or he doesn't know, and he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we think too. So if you could answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will say my question over again, sir. To your knowledge, were the other communicators in the 2nd Battalion qualified or have the knowledge to code or decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in July 1995, the specific period that we will now be addressing, did you have any knowledge in the days following the fall of Srebrenica that Muslim prisoners were held in the Rocevic School at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you share with us exactly what you heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I only heard that there were some prisoners at Rocevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that moment, during that period, were these rumours ever confirmed, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Confirmed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Confirmed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Confirmed to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the time, did you hear any rumours as to what happened to these prisoners, if there were any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And today, sir, do you know if there were prisoners held in Rocevic in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that over television -- on television since I moved to Serbia at some point and that's where I reside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you learn happened to these prisoners in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: That there were executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move back to July 1995, as a communicator, have you ever become aware in the days following the fall of Srebrenica of a telegram being received by the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the same period, did you hear any rumours about a telegram being received by the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the same period, were you made aware at any time that pressure was exercised on your battalion commander or battalion to provide soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know who Sreco Acimovic was?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see him from time to time at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did Sreco Acimovic ever tell you about a telegram received at the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know who Mitar Lazarevic is?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He was in the personnel department of the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember where he worked?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the battalion command in Malesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see Mitar Lazarevic from time to time during this period?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Mitar Lazarevic ever tell you or provide information to you concerning a telegram received at the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know who Vujo Lazarevic is?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Vujo was in the 2nd Battalion in charge of morale of the soldiers and the battalion in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where did Vujo Lazarevic work?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the battalion but he spent most of his time at the lines with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Vujo Lazarevic ever tell you or inform you about a telegram being received at the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we look at the battalion command where you were, how many people were there working in that area where you worked, not only the communication centre but the battalion command itself?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly but in the rear there were five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what do you mean by the rear?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the cooks and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, were there any drivers located in the same area where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were there any other tradesmen working at the battalion command, that you remember of?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any others. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, did you during that specific period in the days following the fall of Srebrenica hear any rumours about the existence of a telegram being received by the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to a different area, sir. Did you know during this period or during the war, let's take a longer period, who was Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How much did you know Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Drago Nikolic for the first time in 1993 when he negotiated with the Muslim side concerning my brother who had been taken prisoner. That's when I saw him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you know what was the position of Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how often did you see him after this period in 1993 that you describe?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him at all after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know Drago Nikolic enough at the time to be able to describe him?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him then for the first time but to me, he still looks the same. Nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how is that, sir? What did he look like at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He was young, only his hair turned grey but that was it. He was of medium height.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about a Muslim exchange of prisoners. I would like now to show you a document which is document 7D454. If you look in the screen in front of you, sir, a document will appear. And this document is in your language. And I would like to have the second page of the document, there's a paragraph numbered 2. Do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I will do now is I will read this second paragraph in English for the record and at the same time as I read you can look on the screen in front of you in your language. Paragraph 2: "Negotiations of the chief of intelligence and security affairs with the Muslim side regarding the exchange. The chief for intelligence and security affairs, 2nd lieutenant Drago Nikolic, met with representatives of the command of the 106th Muslim brigade in the area between Pecine and Kovacevici hours on 7 November 1993 to discuss the exchange of recently captured Rist Todorovic from Rocevic. The enemy side gave a list of persons it was interested in and an agreement was reached to continue contacts on the exchange. Contacts are still underway and our side has its own proposals for the exchange. Specific to these two contacts is that they were the first direct contacts between the two enemy command at such a high level. We expect these contacts to build the enemy's confidence in our fairness and honest intentions." Sir, my first question is do you know Risto Todorovic from Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Risto Todorovic is a cousin of mine on my aunt's side. The only mistake is that he isn't from Rocevic, he is from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this paragraph that I just read out, is that the exchange that you were talking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge what was the result of this exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: It was concluded successfully. They were exchanged. Risto came over to our side and two of their soldiers went to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see Drago Nikolic at any point after this situation in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see him in or around the battalion command or the 2nd Battalion command in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move to the last part of my examination-in-chief. My first question I would like to ask you is you mentioned there were a number of communicators. My question is were they -- were most communicators younger or the same age as you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them were younger, whereas some of them were older than me. Both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when is the first time that you met with anybody from the team for the Defence of Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty days before arriving in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, how do you feel about giving evidence in this trial today?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You believe that testifying here will have repercussions on you when you return home?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't see the relevance of that question in relation to the issues at hand before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we should discuss this in front of the witness. Will you move to your next question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, those are my last two questions, and I believe they're -- if he wants to remove his earphones, I can explain why they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand English, Mr. Cvijetinovic? I'm talking to you. Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly remove your headphones for a short while, please. Yes. Could you answer Mr. Vanderpuye's query or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, for the Defence of Drago Nikolic it's highly relevant a witness to comes here to testify and he testifies in public session. To ask him how he feels and whether he believes there will be repercussions about his testimony when he returns home is highly relevant for himself and for his testimony but also in light of what happened yesterday where another witness refused to testify because he believes that something will happen to him if he returns home, it is highly relevant for the Court to hear it and it's in the interest of justice to know what this witness believes and what his motivation is to come here today and there are only two questions about this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By majority vote once more could you -- yeah. Mr. Cvijetinovic, could you answer the question. The only relevance we see is as regards this witness's credibility, so we are allowing question by majority. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Should I repeat the question, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I can remember it quite vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer the question or do you wish me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you believe that testifying here will have repercussions on you when you return home?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why is this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Because I live in Serbia, I seldom go there, only to meet my neighbours. There's no need for me to feel threatened in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what do you think, sir, today of these events and the war and the events of July 1995? What is your feeling today about these events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What importance do you attach to all this? At the end of day, who he is? Why should we know what importance he attaches to those events?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I must admit, Mr. President, I'm surprised that the Court is not interested in finding out how the witness feels, but I will stop here, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I shan't cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic you had asked for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's probably Mr. Ostojic's mistake, not yours. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No mistake here. We offered no time which we don't need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to ask the witness one question of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Witness, today at page 12, lines 19 to 21 when describing how you would deal with an incoming telegram, you said between the communications centre and the battalion we used a telephone line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I received a telegram from the brigade command, I relay it to the battalion command over the phone in turn because I say the words and the duty officer at the battalion writes them down. He is on the phone and I'm on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So it would follow, to clarify some earlier answers you gave, that there was a telephone at both the communication centre and the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Cvijetinovic. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of Prosecution I'm going to ask you questions in relation to your direct examination, and if I ask you anything that's unclear just let me know and I'll try to rephrase it in a way that we can both understand each other a little bit better. All right. Now, I'm going to ask you a little bit about this telegram a little bit later on but I just want to be clear about what you are saying. Are you saying that in the days following the fall of Srebrenica, while you were a member of the communications unit of the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade that you didn't receive any communication, telephone call about prisoners at the school in Rocevic? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you had no information whatsoever in those few days following the fall of Srebrenica that there were a good number of prisoners that were actually at that school, between say 500 and 1.000?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: We in the battalion did not have this information at all. I did not have this information at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you seem to recall specifically that you were on duty following the fall of Srebrenica in those first few days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Didn't take any days off, right, between the 11th and the 16th of July? Right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was my turn to work. My shift had just commenced in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't take any days off between the 11th of July and, say, the 16th of July, that's your recollection, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, as a signalsman, it was your training, and you understood of course, that it was your job to handle communications between the battalion and its subordinate units, which is companies and platoons and so forth, and the battalion and the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your function as a signalsman limited to those avenues of communication as between the battalion and subordinate units and the battalion and the brigade, or did you actually have to route communications from the battalion beyond the brigade to other brigades in the corps and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I communicated only with the brigade command, the battalion command, and those who were on the line, the companies, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you would agree with me that there's certain information that can be relayed from the brigade to the battalion that is of significance and importance to the battalion; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you receive any communications about enemy movements, enemy locations at your battalion from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I received information. If any attacks were on the line from the Muslim side or if any sabotage actions were expected, then we would receive this information so that we could be ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did you receive any information concerning the movement of Muslim forces following the fall of Srebrenica, at all, at your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, on that day I received information that our line should be in a state of readiness lest we should be caught by surprise and lest our line should be broken through in an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that day. What day are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the Srebrenica day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. How about subsequent to that day?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Again, that the line should be in a state of readiness lest they should be caught by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you hear anything about the movement of Muslim forces, at all?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that from the direction of Srebrenica they were heading towards Tuzla and that is why our defence lines had to be in a state of readiness. That was the only message that we had received, the message that we were supposed to relay to the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's the only information you got regarding the movement of Muslim forces following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You got no other information concerning your battalion or any other battalions following the fall of Srebrenica with respect to the movement of those forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware that the 4th battalion on the 14th of July 1995 was engaged in combat?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew very little. I really didn't know much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, okay. Well, did your battalion receive any of this information concerning the combat operations of the 4th battalion with relation to the Muslim forces following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know that with respect to the presence of prisoners, Muslim prisoners at schools, that information was relayed to the 4th, the 1st, the 6th battalions concerning their presence at schools, following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, yes or no? He has answered it, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, he is at the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm only asking him if he knows about it. I think that's a reasonable question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have no information whatsoever about information that was received by the 4th Battalion, Lazar Ristic of the 4th Battalion, the deputy commander of that battalion about the position of prisoners in Orahovac on the 14th of July 1995, you don't know anything about that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I was in the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it your testimony there was no communication amongst the battalions with respect to the presence of Muslim prisoners in the Zvornik area, is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that there was no communication amongst the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade with respect to the presence of Muslim prisoners in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you had no information with respect to the disposition of any other battalion in the Zvornik area in the days following the fall of Srebrenica, that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is my testimony, but I did not have to know that. I didn't have to know anything about what was going on in the other battalions because I was in the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were in the 2nd Battalion in the communications unit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All communications to your battalion, according to your testimony, went through you and your unit? All of them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but sir, I received information only from the brigade command and the battalion command, and then I relayed them to the battalion command or the brigade command. I had nothing to do with the other battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, my question is, did you receive information from other battalions? That's all my question is. I don't care whether you have anything to do with them or not, I just want to know whether you received any information from them.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no information whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked the question about what would it take to intercept the line, that is the hard-wire line between the communications centre and the IKM of the battalion; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there could be a disruption of the lines if there was shelling because fragments of shells could damage the line and disrupt the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in the days following Srebrenica did that occur in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling and as a result, the communications were disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the event that the hard-wire line is disrupted, what means do you use to communicate?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: We would immediately go out to fix the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that answer, but what means would you use to communicate?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: There was a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: A Motorola. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There was also an RUP 12; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the RUP 12 was used only when attacks were in progress. When a unit would come under an attack, that's when the RUP 12 was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you are aware that in the days following the fall of Srebrenica, that the 7th Battalion had their communications line go down; right? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: What battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: 7th. Well, I don't know about the 7th because I was in the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the 4th Battalion, do you know that their forward command post was overrun, right, and their communications were also cut? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If my colleague is going to suggest from the evidence that the 4th Battalion command post was overrun, he should put a date on that, because that's later in the time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, I think that is a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just catching up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that the 4th Battalion was overrun at all in the days following Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said you got in contact with the Defence in this case about 20 days ago, or 20 days before you arrived here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I take it you met with them and discussed the subject matter of your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you hadn't spoken to anybody else about the be subject matter of your testimony before you were first contacted by the Defence 20 days ago; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to your meeting with the Defence, who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague didn't say when he is talking about or just in general at least the witness can know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think he said he met 20 days ago, he was contacted 20 days ago, that's the point of reference that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it should be clear enough to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you recall, can you tell us when it was that you met with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date. 20 days before I was due to come here, they came to my place and I gave them a statement and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that was at your house, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sabic [phoen] where I live, at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Mrs. Jelena and Mrs. Navinka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you discussed what you are testifying about today; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you were specifically asked about this telegram; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What were you asked about this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they asked me what kind of telegrams I received and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And it's your testimony that you've never received a coded telegram; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the JNA in the communications unit there, you never dealt with a coded telegram; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You never dealt with a coded telegram during your the time that you served in the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's your testimony that no other person in the battalion signals unit was able to decode a telegram, that's your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you know how all of them were trained; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you served with all of them in the JNA too; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was older than some and younger than others so we didn't all serve -- we didn't all do our national service in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You know someone named Dragan Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the communications section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Commander of the communications section. Was he working on the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as the commander of the communication section, is it your testimony that he didn't have the ability or the facility to decode a telegram? He didn't know how to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I say that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that he didn't know. I know that he didn't know. None of us knew how to do it. We hadn't been trained to decode them. None of us had the requisite training.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that coded telegrams were used or were used during the time that you were in service; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which service, Mr. President, the JNA or in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine July 1995. Is that correct, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While you were in the VRS, during your period of time that you served in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, we never received any coded telegrams. I didn't decode any and I didn't know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is, you know that they were in use at the time that you served in the army, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe in the regular army, but I didn't use them while I was in the JNA. I never used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you've never seen, for example, telegram codes?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 3749, please, in e-court. If I could just go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will be stopping at 15.40 instead of 15.45. That's in a minute's time. Today the end of the sitting will be somewhat earlier than usual because we need to finish before, in other words, we will be finishing at 18.40, that's 20 to 7.00, which means that we need to reduce a little bit the breaks that we have which instead of being 25 minutes duration will be of 20 minutes duration. So I suppose you can stop here for the time being, Mr. Vanderpuye, and continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll meet again in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for planning purposes, I don't know how much longer my colleague intends to take. He indicated a certain time, but for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for reminding us. How much longer, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think I will be more than 20 minutes when we get back. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, for the record, Ms. Nikolic for the Nikolic Defence team is present, as well as Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go to, I believe it's the next page ending 616. Sorry, 617. Thank you. Yeah, if we could go to the bottom of the page, please. Thank you. What you see at the bottom of the page, sir, is codes, telegrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before this document is used we should establish some kind of a basis has the witness ever saw this document before, what is the document in the first place and where does it come from. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still have to see it anyway, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document that came from the Bratunac Brigade, was seized in 1998, and the question that was put to the witness was had you ever seen telegram codes such as the ones depicted here in this particular document? Have you ever seen anything like that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you can see in this document under the term Svemir that this is a code for telegram and it assigns certain numbers to letters right? A is 70, B is 22, C is 14 and so on, so forth; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this and I don't know about this type of sending telegrams, I'll not familiar with it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you've never heard of numbers or letters being coded in the way that's depicted in this particular document as a signals officer, that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He's not a signals officer, he is a communicator, big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I believe -- I'll correct myself. Communicator or signalsman; right? You've never heard of documents, of letters or numbers being coded in this particular way as you see in the screen before you? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just page up just a little bit, and you see this at the top of the screen, this talks about artillery code tables. You've never seen a document reflecting the words "Razgovornik" like you see here, which is a table of these kinds of coded information, have you seen anything like that as a signalsman or a communicator, right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I repeat that I never received such a telegram and I never came across this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is whether you've ever heard of anything like this before, as a signalsman.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as far as you know, nobody in the signals unit in your battalion knows anything about coding done in the way that's depicted in this document, that is, codes for certain terms and codes for certain letters? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So nobody in the communications unit in your battalion has the ability to decode a message in this case, for example --

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- that uses the term 100 referring to a code table by the name of MEDA, nobody could understand that that is a code?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as you are aware, nobody in your battalion had that ability, that is to decode or understand coded communications? Nobody in the communications battalion, nobody in the area of security or anything of that nature; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as you know, of course. Yes. Yes, Mr. Bourgon, if you wish to add anything to what I said, please go ahead. Mr. Cvijetinovic, if you could answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, as far as these people in the communications department, we were not able to handle coded telegrams. I don't know about the command battalion, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say you don't know about the command battalion, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the commander, assistant commander and others who worked at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't know whether they had the ability to decode information?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know, and I don't think they knew how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, we talked a little bit about, well, a little while ago we talked about the possibility of the line going down between the IKM and the communications centre. You said it's possible if there's an instance of shelling, for example; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's also possible that that line could be tapped or listened in on?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: They could not listen on -- listen in because the line between the forward command post and the communication companies was in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, they could be in your territory and you not know about that, isn't that right, Mr. Cvijetinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you do know that you didn't know that they were in the schools; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the question. You are mentioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is about my colleague could clarify his question where he says I don't not know that they did not know that they were in the school, I mean, can he clarify his question so that the witness can answer a right question. What is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You say that the line can't be tapped because it's in your territory; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in order for it to be tapped, an enemy would have to be in your territory to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what I'm putting to you, sir, is that you did have enemies in your territory that you admit you didn't know about, in the days following the fall of Srebrenica; right? They were at the school; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't raise your voice unnecessarily, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, I was a little too close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear from you for the first time that -- I've only just learned about such information. I had no knowledge of it prior to this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's my point Mr. Cvijetinovic. What information am I bringing to your attention for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: That there were Muslims, I mean, enemies in our territory able to wiretap. I'm not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You know today that there were in fact prisoners in the school in Rocevic; right? While you were --

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you have said today that you did not know, or you had no information that they were there at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so I put it to you that if you didn't have that information, isn't it possible that you wouldn't have other information relating to whether or not your lines had been tapped by the enemy? Isn't that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I had no such information that the enemy was listening in. It is possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all my question is, is whether or not it's possible. And it is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, are you done with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read the title so that I can catch the meaning of it. What does MEDA mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My understanding is that MEDA refers to the name of the code, that is the code that applies to this table. Svemir applies to the table that is for the telegram codes so that which code is being used is clear to the person decoding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. I think it's MEJA and not MEDA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague can testify where these codes were used, who was using them, what table it is, what date it is, where does it come from. We have no such information and the witness has never seen this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I haven't put the question to the witness as to whether or not he used this document and I'm sure my colleague well understands it and if he wants to redirect the witness on it, I'm sure he's welcome to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- with the permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you know the meaning of the second title in the lower part, "Svemir Sifra Za Telegrame."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. We don't have the English translation up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise for that. I thought we did. The second part reads, telegram codes, Svemir, and that is the name that applies to that telegram code.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how does my colleague know that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed, please. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've testified, sir, that you didn't get any information whatsoever concerning the fact that there were prisoners either on their way or in the school in Rocevic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which means that that information couldn't have gone from your unit to your command or your commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't forwarded and I did not receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you received no information that transportation was needed in order to move these prisoners from the school to another location; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You got no information that personnel were required in order to secure these prisoners at the school?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You got no information that personnel were required to secure these prisoners and escort them for the purposes of being executed?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you got no information that these prisoners were executed?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you got no information that members of your battalion knew about that execution?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... participated in it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That means that your commander didn't have any of the information that would have come to you over the communications line?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Not via our section. He didn't receive such information through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that he testified that he did receive that information through the signals unit?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I did hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where did you hear of it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it there, in Serbia where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear it because you followed the proceedings, or did you hear it because somebody told you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I was told by the Defence that Sreco was here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you told by the Defence what he testified to?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did they say anything about his testimony about a telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did they mention to you that Mitar Lazarevic testified also?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear of it. They didn't mention Mitar Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the first time you heard that name Mitar Lazarevic from anyone from the Defence was when Mr. Bourgon asked you about him on your direct examination today? That's the first time you heard that name from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. The first time what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first time you heard the name Mitar Lazarevic mentioned by the Defence, was that when Mr. Bourgon asked you about him on your direct examination not an hour ago?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the Defence had never mentioned to you Mitar Lazarevic at all, right, before today?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
