utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you spoke to the Defence about 20 days ago, I think that's what you said. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You talked about your commander, Mr. Acimovic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I did not discuss with the Defence about my commander or anyone else. The Defence only talked to me about communications and telegrams. That was the topic of our discussion and that's why I'm here. I absolutely know nothing of anything else. What I told you is what I stand by as I said to the Defence. I'm telling you the same thing, I know nothing of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm curious, I received a note from the Defence and in that note they say that you provided the following information, and the information that you provided was that at the time of the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995 you were on duty for seven days, in that period the witness, that is you, received no coded telegrams requesting Commander Acimovic to select a squad for execution of prisoners, and the communicators in the 2nd Battalion either before or after 1995 never received coded telegrams, and that you weren't trained to receive such telegrams; right? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the course of that conversation with the Defence, you never spoke about Sreco Acimovic, that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. There was no need to mention him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just bear with me for a moment. Did you learn that Sreco Acimovic testified in this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who did you learn that from?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I learned of it here. I learned that he was here for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question was asked and answered before and the answer of the witness was exactly I was told by the Defence that Sreco was here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but he's saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is now saying that he wasn't told by the Defence. Anyway, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: From the Defence appearing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who? Who? From Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you learn at any time that Mr. Acimovic had mentioned that he received a telegram in relation to his testimony in this case? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say the Defence, do you mean Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he also tell you that Mr. Acimovic said that that telegram was coded?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he tell you that Mr. Acimovic said that coded telegram was received by the signals unit?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you that Mr. Acimovic said that the signals unit decoded the telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you when the telegram was supposedly or supposed to have been received?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you what date Mr. Acimovic says he received that telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't mention a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he mention to you whether or not anybody else had testified about that telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And who did he mention had testified about that telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Mitar Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he told you that 20 days ago when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about what Mitar Lazarevic said about that telegram, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: That he confirmed what Sreco had said. I can't quote the exact words, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. He said -- you said he told you that Mitar Lazarevic testified about that telegram; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you think that you could be in trouble for passing on a telegram that called for an execution squad to be assigned?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely did not receive or send such a telegram; therefore, I don't know why I would be in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have a specific recollection that it wasn't received; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you think you could be in trouble for passing on a telegram such as that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say this again, I don't think that I would be in trouble because I did not send any telegrams at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I just have 65 ter 312 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there an English translation of this in e-court? If we could go to page 2, the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under number 4, do you see your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could slide over on the B/C/S, please. I don't know if it's possible to make it smaller so we could see the dates on the top. Maybe we could just look at the B/C/S version, then. I think it would be easier. Do you see your name, number 4, under 13 July?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... indicate?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What does the symbol indicate that's depicted next to your name under the date of 13 July?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There are pluses and minuses here. Probably whoever put this in put it there in order to indicate when I was present and when I was on leave or absent. Whoever put in those pluses and minuses knows best what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, what it shows is the letters "OD," which mean that you were off on that day.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the second date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When I asked you if you were working the whole time, you said you were? Do you remember that too?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, yes. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It also shows that your commander was there, right, on the 14th of July? That's in the top.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It also shows that Mitar Lazarevic was there on the 14th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He's number six --

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- on this list? You see that, right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Is there redirect, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I've just been informed that the document that has been -- last document used is under seal. So did we broadcast or not? Yeah, we did. So we need to block that. We've got a 30-minute -- transcript, I don't know. I would like to have a feedback from Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Vanderpuye on this. I would rather play it safe and redact that as well. I don't know why it is under seal but it seems to be under seal. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as long as it's under seal, I would ask that it remain that way. I can't remember why it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember either. The thing is that if it is correct that it is under seal, we have to respect that. The blocking of the broadcast, external broadcast, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are looking into it right now. Hopefully, we'll be able to tell you in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you here because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are checking, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And in the meantime think on whether we should redact also the text from the transcript. Well, actually I don't see why we should redact because it only refers to him. Actually the questions that were put only refer to him, but there are other individuals there. I don't know why we put it under seal if we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are unable to tell you right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let's play it safe. The transcript I don't see the need for any redaction. You don't know either. So let's play it safe. We redact the broadcast insofar as it was shown. That's the only thing we need to redact or block. Okay. All right. Otherwise the transcript I think it's safe as it is. No other persons, no other names were mentioned. All right. Sorry to interrupt you like this, Mr. Bourgon. Please go ahead with your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, do you remember that the first person you met from the Defence of Drago Nikolic was our investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know that my colleague is on redirect but I don't think that's an excuse to lead the witness. I object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But come on, I mean, let's restrict the objections to substantial ones. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: First, do you recall whether I was there 20 days ago when you met with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember if the first contact you had with the Defence whether Ms. Nikolic beside me was there?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was there, to your knowledge, a first meeting before that when you met somebody else from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, how many meeting, how many times you met with the Defence before you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: There was only one meeting before my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you provided the first information to the Defence of Drago Nikolic to the fact that there was no telegram received at the 2nd Battalion command concerning executions, when this information you first mentioned that, do you recall if before you mentioned that there was ever any mention of the testimony of Acimovic or anyone else in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: The first information I got was from the Defence when we met 20 days ago, and before that I did not have any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is the first information that you gave to the Defence? The first thing that you said before we gave you any information?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my information regarding telegrams and communications, I confirmed, as I have confirmed here, that I did not receive any telegrams containing such text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Radovan Keslelj?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember meeting with Radovan Keslelj at your place?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall that when you met with Radovan Keslelj, Ms. Nikolic was not there?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember that Radovan Keslelj was alone when he saw you?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will need to have a little short break. I will get the notes from the investigators which I will show to the witness and file them before the Court so we know exactly what was said when the investigator took the notes so I can put that to the witness so he can confirm that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How short?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very short, I just need to get a photocopy so I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's handy, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, it's not very far. We have it on the screen here, in our records, we just have to print it and show it to the witness to say exactly what was asked of him and what he said on that day to our investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you make -- yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to have an opportunity to look at the documents, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And secondly, I don't believe that the witness has laid the foundation to have his recollection refreshed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what we were getting to. Mr. Bourgon, you need first to lay precisely the foundation that Mr. Vanderpuye is obviously referring to. And perhaps you have a spare copy for Mr. Vanderpuye or if you don't you can let him have a look at the notes before you put the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Unfortunately I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have one copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Only one copy was delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is understandable in the circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I can -- I have no problem in waiting a few minutes to get more copies so that everyone can get a copy of this. I have no difficulty whatsoever, Mr. President, and I will establish the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's only Mr. Vanderpuye who's interested. I don't figure out that the other Defence teams have any interest at all. But if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Should we wait until we have a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at least for Mr. Vanderpuye. In the meantime, you can ask the foundation questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I need my copy to ask the foundation questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Have a look at them, Mr. Vanderpuye, please. All right. Can we proceed? Mr. Vanderpuye, have you returned the document? Yes, let's give Mr. Vanderpuye two minutes to go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, first you mentioned to my last question that you did -- you do remember meeting with the investigator from the Defence Radovan Keslelj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember what Radovan Keslelj asked you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He also asked me about communications and about telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember if he asked you on that occasion whether you had any -- whether you were -- or where you were at the time of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember if the investigator asked you whether you were on duty during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember that he asked you if you remembered any other communicators who work with you at the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did ask but we didn't talk that much. He talked to me mostly about the documents afterwards over the phone. This was just a brief meeting in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember that the investigator asked you questions about what you knew, if you knew anything about the use of coded telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before that did he tell you that there were no coded telegram? Did he suggest anything to you before asking that question?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that I never received any such telegrams --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know if there was a last part of the answer. I didn't hear anything, but could you finish your answer or repeat it please, Mr. Cvijetinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave a statement to Mr. Keslelj about telegrams and communications. He didn't ask any questions, any further questions because this was just a brief meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did he ask you if you knew Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did he suggest to you at any point what to answer?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like now to show to the witness this document. I think I've established some basis for the document so that the witness can read the document and confirm whether any information included therein was not provided by him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we discuss this in the presence of the witness or not? I prefer not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, can you remove your headphones, please. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't believe that my colleague has laid the foundation to refresh the witness's recollection, he hasn't indicated that he has not recalled anything and there's no basis otherwise to show him the document, certainly not for the purposes of confirming the information that's contained in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is challenging directly the credibility and the integrity of the Defence, and they are using this, if I can say, a tactic I've never seen in the courtroom before in order to attack the credibility of the witness who is before you, and it is normal for that witness to see the information he provided to the investigator who was the first person to see him so that he can confirm whether he provided that information before he spoke to any members of the Defence team. This has got two reasons, of course to re-establish the credibility of the witness which is the purpose of my redirect examination, so show that there was no reason for him to lie in any way but to confirm the information that he provided to the Defence before he spoke to any member of the Defence team. This is a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate that. I don't necessarily wish to dignify the comments that my colleague has made with respect to the tactics that are involved in cross-examination of the witness. But I would like to remind the Court that the information that my colleague is seeking to rehabilitate the witness with is information that was not provided to the Prosecution and had it been provided to the Prosecution, there may not be the need for this redirect examination to begin with. The witness has not indicated that he met with an investigator when those questions were directly put to him as to his contacts with the Defence in this case. That's not a tactic. And the witness simply answered that he had met with the Defence on one occasion. My colleague is now trying to establish something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your final comments, Mr. Bourgon, and let us decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are notes from the investigator. They are not given to the Prosecutor. It is a byproduct of our own work such as like the notes of the Prosecution investigators are. We never get the notes from the investigators that are compiled by the Prosecution investigators. Now they use documents in this cross-examination, documents that were never put on their list before that were never disclosed to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is such low tactics coming from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that this witness must be given an opportunity to see whether he gave that information to investigator in the first place. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keep cool. Don't get keyed up, there's no need to get keyed up with us because we can handle any situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Big deal, a storm in a teacup. We see your point, Mr. Vanderpuye, and in common law terms you are probably a hundred percent right, but this is a mixed system and I think considering the areas that -- the instances when the witness was hesitant not exactly knowing the circumstances, we would rather allow the question by a majority vote. So Mr. Bourgon, please proceed and let us get it over and done with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, first I'd like to apologise -- can you hear?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to apologise for this conversation but I think I did warn you that there would be such a thing and not to worry about it. Do you recall me saying that to you?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would now show you a document, ask the court usher to show you a document. And maybe the best thing would be for everybody to put it on the ELMO beside you. Sir, we'll put the document just on the machine beside you. And I just ask you that you read this document and I will read it in English in the meantime. And it's called information report submitted by Radovan Keslelj, investigator in the defence team for Drago Nikolic. It says a conversation with Cvijetinovic, Milisav and it talks about a conversation on 17 and 26 August 2008. And the participants are identified as investigator Radovan Keslelj and the place is Sabac in Serbia. Information paragraph, "On 17 and 26 August investigator Radovan Keslelj spoke to Cvijetinovic, Milisav from Sabac on his knowledge in relation to events in July 1995. When the war started in BiH the witness was temporarily working abroad in Israel but he returned in September 1992 and was mobilised to the Kiseljak Battalion as a soldier on the Defence lines. After his brother got killed on 22nd March 1993 the witness was withdrawn from the line and was deployed as a communicator in the 2nd Battalion in the Zvornik Brigade, this while he was serving his military service in JNA, he was a communicator. The witness remembers that the time of the action on Srebrenica in July 1995, he was a communicator in the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, the command of which was in Malesic and the commander of which was Sreco Acimovic. He remembers that at the time after the fall of Srebrenica he was on duty as a communicator in the command of the 2nd Battalion in Malesic but he cannot remember who was also a communicator working with him in the shift. He thinks that the communicators change at the same time when there was a shift of the soldiers on the line. Besides him communicators in the 2nd Battalion were Miodrag Pisic, Govan [phoen] Ilic, Stevanovic Dragan, Stambi [phoen]. The communicators at the battalion command never received coded telegrams. The witness said they never received coded telegrams but only connected the communications. At the battalion they never used coded messages and he never decoded any messages. And also other communicators at the battalion were not trained for decoding. When asked whether he had any knowledge about a telegram arriving to battalion requesting to appoint soldiers, volunteers who would carry out execution of prisoners, the witness responded that he never received or heard about such telegram or order. He remembers that at the time after the fall of Srebrenica when the column of Srebrenica people was moving towards the territory of the BiH Federation Vinko Pandurevic called battalion command and said to strengthen the Defence lines and state of readiness in case of an attack. He never heard from Pisic or Ilic or anyone else that the telegram arrive requesting soldiers for execution. The witness says he did not send a telegraph to the brigade informing the brigade that the battalion has no people for execution and he never heard anything about that. The witness says that he never knew Drago Nikolic personally but he know who he looked like at the time. He was young but had grey hair. He remembers that Drago Nikolic came to IKM in Vitinicka Pecina and that he negotiated with the Muslim side to exchange Rist o Todorovic who was captured by Muslims. Those negotiations lasted for several days but Drago managed to carry out an exchange. Risto Todorovic was a cousin of the witness. This exchange took place in December 1993." Sir, my question is the following: do you recall providing this information to Mr. Radovan Keslelj?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you provided this information before you met with any lawyers on the team of Drago Nikolic? That means Jelena Nikolic and myself Stephane Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I met him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there any information that I just read out from this report that was suggested to you by Mr. Keslelj?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall that five minutes before testifying I went to see you in the witness room in the back?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember that for the first time I would ask you the question whether Sreco Acimovic gave any information to you concerning a telegram that he sent -- concerning a telegram that would have been received at the 2nd Battalion concerning a request to send people to participate in executions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again please decide whether what you are going to say should be, ought to be said in the presence or the absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It shouldn't be in the presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then Mr. Cvijetinovic, could you remove the headphones again, please. My apologies for the inconvenience. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question is leading. This is precisely the issue upon which my colleague is seeking to rehabilitate the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is definitely leading. If you could rephrase it, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I would say at this point that the cat is out of the box. I don't know that my colleague can rephrase it in a manner that wouldn't have influenced the witness's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Bourgon has a lot of cats in the bag. So he can make use of one of them. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, before the witness puts back, the Prosecution started the process by challenging again I say the credibility and the integrity of the Defence. I do not appreciate, my colleague does not appreciate and we need to clear the record not only for our name, we never suggested any information to the witness. He cannot hear what I'm saying right now. We never tried to influence this witness in any way. And I think that what the Prosecution suggested to the witness was inappropriate and that's what I'm trying to correct right now. And I did ask a new question to the witness five minutes before walking in the courtroom and I think it is quite appropriate for the witness to tell us what questions I told him five minutes before walking in the courtroom that I asked of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring this to an end. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the questions that were put to the witness concerned his contact with the Defence as concerns his testimony. There is no implication the Defence did anything improper. It was simply to establish the fact that he had contact with the Defence or had information concerning the be subject matter of his testimony which is exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That may be true. I don't even want to discuss that but obviously the questions were put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My hunch is that by now the witness would have even forgotten what the question was, so if you could perhaps rephrase it and be careful how you rephrase it, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to know better how much he remembers, I suppose if you just put a simple question, when I met you five minutes before, what did I mention to you, what did we speak about. I think leaving it that vague, we'll see what he answers and then we'll be in a better position to make an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I put a question to you earlier saying that you recall that we met five minutes before this court session began and you said yes. Do you recall what we discussed then?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you say the names of the three people that we discussed, three names that we discussed that I would be asking questions about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, this is leading in itself again. I mean, try to elicit an answer without putting leading questions, please, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What persons did we speak about, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: We talked about Vujo Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. My memory doesn't seem to be working right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Could you please ask him whether he wishes to have a break, in which case we'll have the break now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a break would be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have 20 minutes and then we'll proceed right through until 18.40. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. --- Break taken at 5.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have last asked him whether you had discussed or you had talked about Vujo Lazarevic and then anybody else and he said I don't know and his memory was failing him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will move on to a different topic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, sir, I only have a few more questions for you and this will be over. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One of my colleagues put a question to you earlier to the effect that there was a telephone line in both the battalion command and the communications centre. What kind of telephone are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: It's a military induction phone that you start up with a lever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And all the questions that were put to you today, the communications between the brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. Your colleague Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. One word was not translated it was "zicani."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which means what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Wire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for this missing word.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, all the communications that we discussed today between the brigade command and the battalion command, on what kind of telephones or telephone lines were these communications taking place?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Wire, by wire. Through a switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are these the same type of military inductor phones?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague showed you a document with some type of coding or codes or letters. Did you at any time within the communications centre of the 2nd Battalion see any book or piece of paper with codes like this on them?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I think I said three or four times that we didn't have such a thing. We didn't work with coded telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague asked you a question about information concerning the movement of troops, and you said that you received telegrams about ensuring that the companies would be in the highest state of readiness. My question is, how many such telegrams do you recall receiving during those days?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember how many, but at least two or three. They were there to warn the lines to be on the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall any other types of telegram that you received while you were working as a communicator?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you receive any telegrams, for example, concerning list of equipment that would be required?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Daily we would receive such things, for example, from the logistics command that would concern supply in terms of food and clothing. That's what we would usually receive, although I can't tell you any exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can have in e-court, please, document P312. And I'd like to have, to begin with, the first page of this document. While the document is being put before you, sir, I have another question. You just responded to my question that you would usually receive telegrams from logistics command concerning supply but that you cannot remember the exact dates. My question is, if you had ever received or been made aware of a telegram asking people to participate in executions, is this something that you would remember?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard of such a telegram, I never received it and I'm not familiar of such a -- with such a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, my question was not precise enough. If such a telegram existed, would you remember such a telegram? If it existed?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Had it existed, I would have remembered it. Much like I remember now that I didn't receive any such telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now we have the document before you. If you can look on the screen before you, I'd just like to draw your attention to the list of names that are there. If I draw your attention and I will read out those names. Sreco Acimovic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Stevo Savic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I will go more quickly. Is there anybody on that list, do you recall that those people you work with them in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I think and we all think this is the document which we said was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President. I think it should not be broadcasted and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have in the meantime, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Vanderpuye, we did our researches as well to see how come it was under seal, and the circumstances are such that for the purpose of this testimony in particular, we don't need it to remain under seal at all and we can lift the confidentiality, so that's precisely what we are doing. Okay. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, we can look at this document that is before you. And the names of the people that appear in -- beside the numbers 1 to 16, do you recall working with these people in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Some were there but I don't remember all of them. I don't know which of them was in the command during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And coming from any of them that you do remember, did any of these people ever provide you with any information concerning a telegram received at the 2nd Battalion requesting people to participate in executions?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look down at the bottom of this document, you have the list of the communicators. Do you recognise the names of the eight communicators who are there?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Stevanovic, he is the commander. My question to you concerning Stevanovic, did he operate the switchboard or it was only communicators who operated the switchboard?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: He did too. He only commanded the squad but he did the same things we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did any of these people, these communicators that are on that list, did any of them provide you any information or even rumour concerning a telegram that was received at the 2nd Battalion requesting people to participate in executions?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question, sir, is simply, coming here today, do you have any reason why you would not tell all the truth about this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No reason. What I had to say, I did and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you very much, and I apologise for the times that you had to remove the earphones. This is normal proceedings between lawyers but I inform you of that. So thank you very much, sir, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with leave of the Court I have just a few questions to put this to witness with respect to the document he was shown. I know it's extraordinary to ask to recross a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The questions I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you please -- first, again you will have to suffer a little bit more, Mr. Cvijetinovic. Could you please remove again your headphones, please. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, we would like to know what the questions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first has to do with what's indicated in the report, that he spoke to this investigator on two separate occasions and my information is or my understanding is he has only met with him on one occasion. I wanted to know whether he met on one or more occasions. The second has to do with whether or not he had any information concerning the fact that Mr. Acimovic had testified and the subject matter of his testimony before he met the investigator since that was unknown to me during my cross-examination initially that he ever even met an investigator. The third question has to do with the specific reference that he made in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can lift it, lift it up as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are right, because if I remove my headphones I can barely hear you while I hear everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise for that, Mr. President. The third question has to do with, well, really his recollection because it says in the statement itself that he remembers that he was on duty but he cannot remember who was also a communicator working with him in the shift which he apparently seems to recall at this time. And the last question has to do with a specific recollection of Vinko Pandurevic calling the battalion command in reference to strengthening the lines in the state of readiness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to comment, Mr. Bourgon, before we decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As long as the my colleague is asking these questions and they are questions that were not raised and not discussed at all during the either examination-in-chief or cross-examination and these are completely new questions. I understand that they are raised on this document but this document was used for the purpose of for a very, very limited purpose. So the first two questions, I have no problem because they are a link to why the document was used in the first place, how many times he met, whether he had information about Acimovic before, I have no problems. When he gets into the contents of the information itself, if the Court allows it I have no problem, but this was new information that should not be asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may well be if the last of these questions is to be gone into, then I'm going to ask for the leave to discuss the matter with my client, have the witness come back tomorrow morning, and ask some further questions in cross-examination. I think we've probably reached the point with this witness where enough is enough, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I consider those words of wisdom, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is to allow the first two questions only. We see no need or regularity in allowing the second and the third. The third and the last, sorry. So it's the first and second question only.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, I just have a couple of questions for you. You were shown a document by my colleague Mr. Bourgon which is denominated as an information report in it. In paragraph one it indicates that you on the 17th and 26th of August spoke to Radovan Keslelj in regards of this matter. Now, did you meet with him on two separate occasions as well or did you simply speak to him on two separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: We met the first time when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which of those two dates would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he identify himself, by the way, as an investigator for the Defence when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On both occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the time that you spoke to him, did you have any information about the fact that Sreco Acimovic had testified in this case about having received a telegram and about knowing about the prisoners in Rocevic School?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV CVIJETINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetinovic, we have come to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you for having been kind enough to come and give testimony here and on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home. Our staff will give you the assistance you require.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, we have the list to which only the information report will be added, the one that we -- that was given to the witness, we did not have time to add this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one you read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think once you have read it out we don't need a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then that's perfectly fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the others -- we don't have a list, so I'm not in a position to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's only 7D454, the documents I used concerning the involvement of Drago Nikolic in exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there's none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other Defence teams? None. So it is so admitted. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have any documents that you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just -- it's just the one document that I used with the witness, 65 ter 3749.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is already tendered, no, I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe I have an English translation for that now for the Court as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I object to the admission of -- the admissibility of this document. 3749 is the document with the code, unless I'm correctly -- if I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a document that the witness does not recognise, knows nothing about. It is a new document and there's no reason to admit this document at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The fact itself that he didn't recognise it is sufficient for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, is what you mentioned the only grounds that you have for objecting to the admissibility of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in addition to this, this is the type of documents concerning communications where we are now in the Defence case, these documents were never disclosed to the Defence, they might have been somehow given in some big collection but they were never disclosed. During the case of the Prosecution, many questions were asked about code, coded telegrams, list of documents. I myself used documents like this during the case with the Prosecution. These documents should have been given to the Defence at that point. The Prosecution is using the ruling of this Court to use any documents in cross-examination to supplement his rule 65 ter list. This is, Mr. President, an objection that I wanted to make for a long time but it didn't touch my client so I refrain because I know the Court doesn't appreciate these objections. I refrain from doing so, but now I will be filing a motion because I believe the Prosecution is using the ruling of the Court to at this moment enter a whole bunch of new evidence that it should have done so during its case in chief. In all these documents, whether they are accepted or not, admitted or not, at the end of the case then they will ask for these documents to be admitted through the bar table. And this reverse process, Mr. President, makes it that this document should not be accepted. Now, specifically with this one, the only reason if the document is accepted, if it's accepted that the witness did not recognise it and not for its content, then I agree it can go in. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague is correct, the document was used for the purposes of establishing whether or not the witness was familiar with this type of document. I think it was very specific in my question of it. The document is not being offered as substantive evidence of the fact that these particular codes were used by the 2nd Battalion or by the Zvornik Brigade even. This is a document that comes from a seizure of the Bratunac Brigade. The Bratunac Brigade apparently has this kind of information. By inference it would suggest that the Zvornik Brigade had similar documents. If he is not familiar with that, he is not familiar with that. We are not offering for that purpose. We are simply offering it for the purpose of showing that these types of coding information were used during the time that he was in service, or I should say in the VRS in the Zvornik Brigade as a communications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Enough, enough, enough, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vanderpuye, you do not have any information when this document was actually in effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just out of curiosity, this document is entitled as "Work Plan of Signal Corps Station Artillery Communication Post Measure." Where did that come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where did the document come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The title in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, the title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution that put that title?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is an English translation I think in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because I didn't see that kind of information from the document itself, work plan of signal corps station.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document itself as far as the English translation is -- I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, there's no English translation, but we have English title in the e-court system which was provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand there actually is an English translation, but it wasn't at the time that I used it, to be fair, to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is now, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having heard your qualification in response to Mr. Bourgon's questions, we are admitting this document into evidence, but not for the proof of its contents. So anything else? None. We can proceed with the next witness. Next one is Milisav Nikolic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd discussed with my friends raising a quick preliminary before the next witness was brought in. It's something frankly that could be raised in the presence of the witness. However, the Court pleases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And everyone. General Pandurevic has brought to my attention that I made an error yesterday, obviously through counsel, that I made an error yesterday during my cross-examination of Mr. Sakotic. I asked a question, and this is at page 25797 of the record, at line 4: "Well, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from Mr. Ristanovic as well as survivors of a mass execution in the Orahovac area and Mr. Ristanovic testified that he used that backhoe excavator to dig a mass grave while the executions were still going on in front of him, do you know anything about that, sir? And the answer was: "No, not at all," and that was in the context of me showing a particular vehicle work log showing a backhoe excavator July 14th digging trenches at Orahovac for six hours. I made an error when I asked that question and suggested that Mr. Ristanovic had stated in his testimony that he used that particular backhoe excavator on the 14th of July 1995 at Orahovac. In fact, what Mr. Ristanovic testified in Blagojevic was that he used another backhoe excavator, a G700 which was located at the Zvornik Brigade engineering company compound but which was owned by the Zvornik prudevij [phoen] company, Zvornik road company, which is based in Zvornik. So the question I should have asked Mr. Sakotic was, since he had been clear in his Blagojevic testimony that he had used another backhoe was I should have asked him or put it to him that he had used a backhoe excavator at Orahovac on the 14th of July. Not the one that was depicted on the log that I showed him. So I wanted to clarify that for the record. I thank the Pandurevic team for bringing that error to my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I should say thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we give him a punishment, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm thinking of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good evening to you, Mr. Nikolic. And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. That's the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic is going to put some questions to you. She will be followed by others on cross-examination. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening to you, Your Honours. Good evening to you, Mr. Nikolic. We've met before but let me just state my name for the record. I'm Jelena Nikolic and I represent Mr. Drago Nikolic here. Could you please state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Milisav Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of January 1963 in Brano Bacici, Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation, Mr. Nikolic, where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm a construction technician. I work in a construction company in Backa Topola named predemij [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I live in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you married, do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm married and I have two children, a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background? What is your religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm an ethnic Serb. And I am an Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about your wife?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My wife is a Croat and she is a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 3D383 up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a lot of background noise such as typing and --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, could you please look at this document that you see in front of you on the screen. On the right-hand side I think you can see the B/C/S version. And could you please tell us what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is a baptismal certificate of my wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And her name is?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Her name is Ruza and the name she was given at her baptism is Angela.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Her maiden name?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Horvat.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I won't be needing that document anymore, thank you. In the period between 1992 and 1996 were you mobilised into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you related to Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other brothers or sisters apart from Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have an older brother Dragan and a younger brother Borislav, but he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where did you grow up, all of you?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We all of us grew up in the village of Brano Bacici in the Bratunac municipality in our family home where we lived together with our parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe briefly the circumstances in which you grew up, you and your three brothers. What was your family like?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, we grew up in -- we grew up poor in a rural family. My mother was a housewife and my father was a farmer. He would spend his summers working as a construction worker. We had a little bit of land and we worked it, and we children helped do that. And as we grew up, we helped him perform all those jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we go back a decade or so, were your parents able to continue to work and to work the land in the past ten years? What is their health? What has their health been like over the past ten years?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not able to do so because they are ill. As they grow old, they get more and more ill. My father had throat cancer and he had surgery for it in 1986, and my mother had been ill even before that, she had thyroid problem, so because of that, because of their ill health they had been unable to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And how were they able to make ends meet, your parents?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the four of us brothers, we helped them. Depending on what they needed every month, we gave them as much money as they needed. We also gave them food and other items that they needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you provide for them?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not only myself, all of us four brothers, we provided for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us more about your brothers?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, my eldest brother Dragan has a degree in political science from Sarajevo. Before the war he worked in the bauxite mines in Milici. And he currently works in the Bratunac municipality in the municipal office there. And also I have completed the school for construction technicians and I live and work in Novi Sad. My youngest brother Borislav has a degree from the mining engineering faculty in Tuzla. Before the war he also had a job in the Milici bauxite mines. And after the war he worked in the Zvornik quarry until he retired, and then afterwards he died. My brother Drago completed the military high school in Sarajevo. He left for Sarajevo when he was 14. He lived there as a boarder until he completed his school in the military dorm and after that he remained in Sarajevo. He worked there until the beginning of the war when he moved to Zvornik where he worked until he retired in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did Drago spend all his working life as a military professional?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, up to the moment when he was retired in 1998. From the moment he had started the high school education.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why did Drago Nikolic leave home when he was 14 to begin his study at the military high school and who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The deciding factor was our father's decision who was forced to make that decision because of economic necessity. At the same time, my older brother was in attendance of the mining -- or school for mining technology in Tuzla, whereas myself and my younger brother were still in primary school. So our father was unable to finance the education of all of us. As is well known, at the time military schools were free, the state paid for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, for one to be admitted into a military school and to attend a JNA school, did the family have to undergo certain checks including of course the potential student?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly. For someone to be admitted into such a school the family had to be loyal to the then communist system. This meant that no one from the family was allowed to have either a criminal file or even misdemeanour file, and they ran their checks even outside our immediate family. That was one of the preconditions. Another precondition was Drago's good grades in school. I remember well that at the entrance exam he achieved one of the best results.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell us something about the family circumstances of your brother Drago Nikolic's family.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My brother is married. His wife's name is Milena. He had three children, a daughter by the name of Dragona who is now married, mother of one child. Another daughter, Vida with two children, married. And he had a son Dragisa who died when he was eight in 1980 in the Forenza [phoen] Hospital near Sarajevo. 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court 3D382, please. Mr. Nikolic, again you will see a document on the screen. Once it is there, please have a look at it and tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is a death certificate for Dragisa Nikolic, Drago's son.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we will no longer need this document. How did this event influence your entire family?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was a tragic event for the whole family. It was particularly difficult for Drago's immediate family, and for him as well. It is a loss of a child. You can only imagine what that is like. After that there were some changes in the family. They got closer. Although before that he would usually visit us alone. After that he began visiting us with the rest of his family. You could see that he changed physically. Although, up to that point, he had been partially grey in terms of his hair. At that moment he turned completely white.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the relationship between the four brothers and the family?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Our relationship was a brotherly one. We were fair to each other, we respected each other and we felt close. Ever since we were little kids we were raised that way to help each other, to take care of each other by our parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When any of the brothers had particular needs, did the others come to his aid even later on?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly. For example, when I was building my house in Novi Sad, my brothers, Dragan and Drago, took leave, annual leave and arrived together with our father to help me constructing the house, although it was not long after little Dragisa had been buried. When brother Borislav bought a company of his -- bought an apartment of his company and the apartment was not finished at that point. Since he was ill at the time, my brothers and myself agreed that we would finish the apartment. We bore the rest of the costs. Then it seemed to be Drago's turn to deal with his housing situation. He was trying to buy a house in Banja Koviljaca. I remember that Dragan at that time lent him some money to purchase the house. I wasn't able at the time financially to assist him. I know that he lent him some money and later on when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, he needs to actually repeat the last part of the answer. He said, "I wasn't able at the time to assist him financially, I know that he lent him some money and later on when," you said something which the interpreters didn't catch. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He also lent him money when Drago's daughters were getting married.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any time when it's convenient to you, madam, we'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are finishing early as we intimated to you before. We'll resume tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
